title: Occupational extinction: Entrants adjust while incumbents lose
desc: Historical automation eliminated an occupation yet preserved later cohort employment, separating replacement opportunities from displaced-worker harm.

kps.k: Automation can eliminate an entry-level occupation without reducing later cohorts’ employment, while imposing lasting losses on incumbent workers.
kps.d: Answering the Call of Automation distinguishes occupational destruction from population-level employment outcomes. The study estimates that telephone dial cutovers reduced young operator numbers by 50–80%, immediately and permanently eliminating nearly 2% of local jobs held by young, white, American-born women. Yet it finds no detectable employment decline among successive cohorts of young women. This historical evidence qualifies both claims that occupational automation necessarily creates lasting aggregate unemployment and claims that stable employment means workers escaped harm; it does not establish what contemporary AI will do.

qs.q: Cutovers caused a sharp decline in the number of young operators: though the number of young operators was on average growing moderately in the decades before a city’s first cutover to dial, even conditional on overall population—consistent with AT&T’s motivations for adoption (as in Feigenbaum and Gross 2023)—it subsequently dropped by 50 to 80% (Panel A).
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Panel (A) plots the high-frequency event study estimates for the percent of young, white, American-born women who were telephone operators, where it becomes apparent that automating local telephone operation immediately and permanently elim- inated nearly 2% of area jobs for the group.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Incumbents’ losses and later entrants’ adjustment followed different age patterns.
kps.d: Exposed incumbent operators were about eight percentage points less likely to remain telephone-industry operators a decade later. Those aged 26 and above suffered employment losses of roughly seven percentage points; transfers into related telephone jobs absorbed little displacement. Among later cohorts, secretarial and service employment offset most lost operator jobs. Women aged 21–25 more often entered similarly paid secretarial work, while younger women more often entered lower-paid services. Thus employment continuity did not preserve occupational earnings potential. Occupation scores and historical occupation-level wage comparisons are not direct measurements of displaced workers’ wage trajectories.

qs.q: Although the odds of working other jobs in the telephone industry or as a telephone operator in another industry increased modestly after a cutover for women under 25, these effects can only account for a small fraction of overall operator displacement (compare the magnitudes on the cutover interactions in Panel A with Panels B and C).
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Historical comparisons support the employment finding, but identification and precision limit its interpretation.
kps.d: The authors combine archival and newspaper cutover dates with 1910–1940 complete-count censuses, comparing staggered adoption across cities and tracking incumbent women through linked genealogical records. Their main sample includes 2,846 cities, with 261 cutovers by 1940. Matching and reweighting address observable selection, but the linked sample remains nonrandom. Controls, alternative samples and population-growth checks support the authors’ interpretation, without proving adoption was exogenous. Pre-cutover growth in operator employment and possibly secretarial work remains a qualification. The authors can reject unemployment increases equal to the original shock only at just above the 10% significance level. Employment robustness also does not extend uniformly to secondary outcomes: large-city estimates show reduced schooling.

qs.q: For most of the paper, we will focus on the 2,846 cities with ≤100,000 population in 1920 (261 with cutovers by 1940), where subscribers were typically converted to dial all at once.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

qs.q: The set of operators in this sample is inevitably not random.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

kps.k: The study tests competing explanations for adjustment without conclusively identifying the mechanism.
kps.d: The authors find no systematic wage declines in substitute occupations and no increase in the focal group’s occupational shares, weighing against adjustment solely through wage cuts or displacement of other demographic groups. However, wage estimates cannot exclude changes of ±10%, lack a comparable historical panel and do not establish that all workers escaped losses. Occupational-share tests also impose a fixed-total perspective. The authors investigate complementary work, productivity and scale effects, coincident technologies and new uses for labour, but the supplied findings do not establish a single demand-side explanation. Rapid growth in soda-fountain and lunch-counter work is suggestive context, not a demonstrated cutover effect.

qs.q: Moreover, the absence of a detectable effect on wages in substitute occupations suggests against the view that the labor market simply moved down the demand curve in these occupations, settling at higher employment and lower wages.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

qs.q: These results should be interpreted with some caution, given standard errors (we cannot statistically rule out wage changes of ±10%), which may be due to heterogeneous effects, noise in the wage data, or more limited power afforded by a smaller set of cutovers (72 vs.

kps.k: The practical implication is to assess displaced workers, replacement opportunities and job quality separately.
kps.d: Applied to the automation debate, the study supports tracking incumbent employment and occupational losses alongside later entrants’ outcomes rather than using aggregate employment as a sufficient measure of adjustment. Age and prior occupational investment can shape who bears transition costs, while the availability and pay of substitute work shape subsequent cohorts’ prospects. These are analytical implications of the historical findings, not tested policy recommendations or forecasts for legal AI.

qs.q: While some found other jobs in the telephone industry, others (especially older workers) left the workforce, and those who remained were more likely to be in lower-paying occupations.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

vlens.an: The academia-and-research source directly supports the proposition that occupational extinction and aggregate employment adjustment can coexist. Its historical evidence finds that mechanical switching sharply eliminated telephone-operator work, while later cohorts of young women experienced no detectable decline in employment because other occupations absorbed entrants. At the same time, incumbent operators—especially older workers with greater occupational investment—faced persistent displacement, workforce exit and movement into lower-paying work. Material variation therefore lies between cohorts and outcomes rather than in disagreement with the proposition: employment stability for later entrants did not eliminate losses for incumbents or guarantee equivalent job quality. The source also qualifies the strength and scope of the finding through nonrandom linked samples, statistical-power constraints, pre-trend concerns and incomplete evidence on adjustment mechanisms. This is historical evidence, not a forecast of contemporary AI’s effects. Because the corpus supplies one curated academic source here, its position should not be treated as representative of academia generally.

elens.an: The sole curated source for this time-period facet directly supports the proposition’s central distinction between occupational extinction and aggregate employment adjustment. Its historical evidence indicates that mechanical switching sharply eliminated telephone-operator roles and imposed persistent losses on incumbent operators—particularly older workers, some of whom left employment or moved into lower-paying occupations—while later cohorts of young women experienced no detectable decline in overall employment because other clerical and service roles absorbed much of the lost entry-level work. The source also supports the proposition’s internal qualifications: replacement employment differed in quality and by age, related telephone jobs absorbed only a small share of displaced incumbents, and the employment null is subject to identification and statistical-precision limits. This is historical evidence that informs analysis of the 2023–2024 generative-AI shock; it is not a forecast of AI’s effects.
